body:
Scientific reasoning begins with what can be observed

Science explains natural events by examining evidence rather than accepting a statement merely because it sounds convincing. It begins with a question about something that can be observed, measured or otherwise investigated. A scientific explanation must remain open to correction when better evidence becomes available.

An observation is information obtained by careful examination or measurement. An inference is an interpretation drawn from observations.

For example, seeing that a plant has yellow leaves is an observation. Saying that the leaves became yellow because the plant received insufficient nutrients is an inference about the cause. The inference may be reasonable, but different causes are possible; it requires further evidence. Observations can be qualitative, such as noting a change in colour, or quantitative, such as recording a height of 12 cm.

Questions, hypotheses and predictions are different

A good scientific question is specific enough to investigate. The question 'Does the amount of sunlight affect the growth of similar seedlings?' is more useful for a test than the vague question 'Why are plants different?'

A hypothesis is a tentative, testable explanation or proposed relationship. It is not an established fact and is not simply any guess. For example, 'Under otherwise similar conditions, seedlings receiving more sunlight will grow more over 7 days' can be examined through observations and comparisons.

A prediction states what should be observed in a specified test if the hypothesis is supported. In this example, the prediction is that the group receiving more sunlight will show a greater increase in height over the 7 days. The hypothesis gives a proposed explanation; the prediction states an expected observation.

Testing and interpreting a result

A useful school-level description of scientific enquiry is to observe, ask a question, propose a hypothesis, test it and examine the result. A test may involve an experiment, additional observation or measurement. The result may support the hypothesis, oppose it or remain inconclusive. If the result does not agree with the prediction, the explanation or the way it was tested needs reconsideration.

Scientific work is not always a fixed sequence completed only once. New observations may lead to a better question, a revised hypothesis or another test. A result that agrees with one prediction does not prove that an explanation must be true in every situation.

Prelims focus

  • Observation records what is noticed or measured; inference interprets what it may mean.
  • A scientific hypothesis is tentative and testable.
  • A prediction is the result expected under stated conditions if a hypothesis is supported.
  • Testing may use experiments or further observations.
  • Trap: A favourable result supports a hypothesis; it does not make the hypothesis an unquestionable fact.

[Sources: NCERT, Curiosity, Class 6, Chapter 1, 'The Wonderful World of Science', printed pp. 5–7 (chapter transcription consulted on NCERT Solutions website, 2 November 2026).]

title: Scientific Enquiry: From Observation to a Testable Hypothesis

body:
Why a fair comparison matters

A test is useful only if its result addresses the question being asked. Suppose 2 groups of similar seedlings are compared for 7 days. Group A receives 2 hours of sunlight daily, while Group B receives 6 hours. Both receive 100 mL of water daily and, as far as possible, have the same type of plant, similar initial size, soil and pot size. The increase in height is recorded for each group.

Here, sunlight exposure is the factor deliberately changed, often called the independent variable. Height increase is what is measured, or the dependent variable. Water, plant type, soil, pot size and duration are conditions kept comparable, often called controlled variables. Group A provides the lower-exposure comparison condition. Keeping other conditions similar makes it easier to judge whether differing sunlight exposure is associated with the result.

A fair comparison reduces alternative explanations but does not automatically eliminate them. More sunlight may also alter temperature; a careful conclusion states the conditions under which the result was obtained.

Observation, repetition and independent checking

Not every scientific question can be answered by deliberately changing one factor. Weather events, for example, may be studied through repeated observations of rainfall, temperature and time. Such observations can identify patterns even when a controlled experiment is not practical.

A single observation can be misleading because of a mistaken reading, an unusual event or an overlooked difference. Repeated observations help reveal whether a finding occurs consistently. When other people obtain similar results through an independent check, confidence may increase. Repetition and review improve the quality of evidence; neither guarantees that every conclusion is correct.

Scientific observations may be expressed as descriptions or measurements. 'The soil appears dry' is descriptive evidence; 'the water level fell by 3 cm in 2 days' is numerical evidence. Numerical statements are more useful when the measuring method, unit, place and time are clear.

Evidence is not the same as a claim

Statement typeExampleWhat it establishes
ObservationThe measured height increased by 2 cm.A recorded change, if measured reliably.
HypothesisMore sunlight causes greater growth under comparable conditions.A relationship proposed for testing.
Evidence-based conclusionIn this comparison, the higher-light group grew more.What the comparison supports in its conditions.
Unsupported claimMore sunlight always makes every plant grow faster.No universal conclusion follows from one comparison.

A photograph, an advertisement, a personal story or a famous person's assurance can suggest a question, but it does not by itself establish a general scientific conclusion. A claim needs evidence relevant to that exact claim. An unsupported claim is not necessarily false; it is simply not adequately established by the information presented.

Association does not by itself establish a cause

If 2 quantities rise together, they are associated, but that alone does not show that one caused the other. For example, both the sale of cold drinks and the use of fans may increase on hotter days. It would be mistaken to conclude merely from this pattern that buying cold drinks causes people to use fans; hot weather can affect both. To make a causal claim, other plausible explanations must be considered.

Prelims focus

  • Independent variable: the factor being changed or compared.
  • Dependent variable: the result being observed or measured.
  • Controlled variables: other relevant conditions kept comparable.
  • Repeating observations can reveal unusual or mistaken readings.
  • Association is not sufficient proof of causation.
  • Trap: A personal example or a photograph is not automatically evidence for a universal claim.

[Sources: NCERT, Curiosity, Class 6, Chapter 1, printed pp. 5–7 (chapter transcription consulted on NCERT Solutions website, 2 November 2026); Smithsonian Learning Lab, Next Generation Science Standards, 'Planning and Carrying Out Investigations', grades 3–5 guidance (consulted 2 November 2026).]

title: Fair Tests, Repeated Observations and the Strength of Evidence

body:
What a measurement tells us

Measurement means comparing a quantity with an agreed unit. A measurement has a numerical value and a unit: in '12 cm', the number is 12 and the unit is centimetre. Without the unit, 'the length is 12' is incomplete. Choosing a suitable unit also makes information easier to compare.

Before standard units became common, people used the length of a foot, a forearm or a handspan. Such measures vary from person to person. For example, a 60 cm desk might measure 4 handspans for a person with a 15 cm handspan and 3 handspans for another person with a 20 cm handspan. The desk has not changed; the chosen units differ. A standard centimetre scale describes it consistently as 60 cm.

The 7 SI base quantities and units

The International System of Units (SI) provides agreed units for scientific and everyday measurement. It has 7 base units. The unit symbol is important: capital and lower-case letters are not interchangeable.

Base quantitySI base unitSymbol
Lengthmetrem
Masskilogramkg
Timeseconds
Electric currentampereA
Thermodynamic temperaturekelvinK
Amount of substancemolemol
Luminous intensitycandelacd

The SI base unit of mass is kilogram (kg), not gram. The SI base unit of temperature is kelvin (K), written without a degree sign.

Derived units and common everyday units

A derived unit is formed by combining base units. Area uses square metres (m2), volume uses cubic metres (m3) and speed uses metres per second (m/s). The SI unit of force is the newton (N), also a derived unit. In ordinary shopping, people may say 'weight of 1 kg', but kilogram measures mass; in physics, weight is a force measured in newtons.

The litre (L) is commonly used for liquid volume and is accepted for use with SI, although it is not one of the 7 SI base units. Degree Celsius (°C) is a commonly used temperature unit related to the kelvin. A temperature of 0 °C corresponds to 273.15 K, while a temperature rise of 1 °C equals a rise of 1 K.

Prefixes and useful conversions

  • kilo (k) means 1000 times: 1 km = 1000 m and 1 kg = 1000 g.
  • centi (c) means 1/100: 1 m = 100 cm.
  • milli (m) means 1/1000: 1 m = 1000 mm and 1 L = 1000 mL.
  • Time: 1 min = 60 s and 1 h = 3600 s.

Converting before comparing quantities prevents mistakes. For example, 36 km/h is 10 m/s because 36 km is 36000 m and 1 hour is 3600 s. Unit symbols do not take a plural ending: write 5 kg, not 5 kgs.

Why standard measurement matters in India

Standard units are also important in commerce. As described by India's Department of Consumer Affairs on 2 November 2026, the Legal Metrology Act, 2009 has been in force since 1 April 2011. India's legal metrology system standardises measurements used in trade and provides for verification of measuring instruments. This helps make a stated mass or volume comparable for buyers and sellers.

Prelims focus

  • SI has 7 base units; length is measured in m, mass in kg and time in s.
  • Electric current: A; temperature: K; amount of substance: mol; luminous intensity: cd.
  • Area (m2) and speed (m/s) use derived units.
  • 1 km = 1000 m; 1 m = 100 cm = 1000 mm.
  • The litre is accepted for use with SI but is not an SI base unit.
  • Trap: The kilogram measures mass; the newton measures force, including weight.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter 10, 'Motion and Measurement of Distances', printed pp. 97–101, 2018–19 printing; Bureau International des Poids et Mesures, The International System of Units, 9th edition (2019, updated June 2026), 'SI base units' and 'SI Brochure' (consulted 2 November 2026); NIST, Guide to the SI, Chapter 5, 'Units Outside the SI' (consulted 2 November 2026); Government of India, Department of Consumer Affairs, 'Legal Metrology', overview (consulted 2 November 2026).]

title: Measurement and SI Units: A Common Language for Quantities

body:
Match the instrument to the quantity

Useful measurements begin with the correct quantity and an appropriate instrument. A ruler can measure the straight length of a notebook; a measuring tape is more suitable for the girth of a tree; a thread can follow a curved line and then be straightened against a scale. A clock measures a time interval, a thermometer measures temperature and an odometer records a vehicle's accumulated travel distance. A speedometer, in contrast, indicates speed.

Good measurement also requires stating the unit and the conditions. 'The water temperature was 30 °C at noon' is more informative than 'the water was hot', and 'rainfall was 12 mm in 24 hours at one location' is more specific than 'it rained a lot'.

Correct reading of a ruler

A ruler should be placed along the object being measured, and the eye should be positioned directly above the mark being read. Looking from one side can make a mark appear to lie opposite a different graduation; this is called parallax error.

A ruler with a damaged zero end need not be discarded for a simple measurement. Place one end of the object at a clearly visible graduation and subtract the initial reading from the final reading. If one end is at 1.0 cm and the other at 14.3 cm, the length is 14.3 cm − 1.0 cm = 13.3 cm. It is the difference between the two readings, not the final reading alone.

Accuracy, precision and reasonable reporting

Accuracy describes closeness to a correct reference value. Precision describes closeness of repeated readings to one another. The two ideas are related but not identical. Suppose a reference length is 10.0 cm. One instrument gives readings 10.0 cm, 10.1 cm and 9.9 cm; another repeatedly gives 9.2 cm, 9.2 cm and 9.3 cm. The second set is closely clustered, but its readings are consistently below the reference value. Thus a series of nearly identical readings can still be inaccurate.

Small variations can arise from how a reading is taken; a consistently incorrect zero mark may shift every reading in the same direction. Repeating a measurement can expose variable readings, while checking against a reliable reference can expose a consistent error.

The smallest marked division of an instrument also limits what can reasonably be reported. A ruler marked only in centimetres cannot justify an unassisted measurement such as 12.347 cm. Reporting many decimal places does not itself make a measurement more accurate.

Prelims focus

  • To measure length with a damaged zero, subtract the starting reading from the final reading.
  • Parallax error can arise when the eye is not correctly aligned with the graduation.
  • Accuracy concerns closeness to the reference; precision concerns agreement among repeated readings.
  • An odometer records distance travelled; a speedometer indicates speed.
  • Trap: Repeated readings that agree closely can still share a consistent error.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter 10, 'Motion and Measurement of Distances', printed pp. 99–102, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 13, 'Motion and Time', printed pp. 150–151, 2018–19 printing; NIST, 'Accuracy', OSAC Lexicon (dated 15 January 2025; consulted 2 November 2026); NIST Computer Security Resource Center Glossary, 'Precision' (consulted 2 November 2026).]
